request.user:
[2025 summer phd math-stat — problem 2]

Part III, Problem 2 (50 pts). Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with density $p_\theta(\cdot)$; let $l_n(\theta)$ be the negative log-likelihood with Hessian $H_n(\theta)$, regularity conditions satisfied.
(i) To estimate $\psi(\theta)$, state the Cramér-Rao lower bound for any unbiased $T(X)$ with $\mathbb{E}[T(X)] = \psi(\theta)$, and prove your statement.
(ii) Given an initial estimator $\tilde\theta$ with $\|\tilde\theta - \theta\|_2 = o_p(n^{-1/4})$ and $H_n(\theta)$ $L$-Lipschitz, construct the Newton-Raphson (one-step) estimator $\hat\theta$ and show it is asymptotically normal and achieves the Cramér-Rao lower bound. (Hint: you may assume the MLE is asymptotically efficient.)

response.text:
Let the true parameter be denoted by \(\theta_0\in\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d\), and let

\[
L_n(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(X_i),\qquad 
\ell_n(\theta)=\log L_n(\theta),\qquad 
l_n(\theta)=-\ell_n(\theta).
\]

Write

\[
S_n(\theta)=\nabla_\theta \ell_n(\theta)=-\nabla l_n(\theta)
\]

for the score and

\[
H_n(\theta)=\nabla^2 l_n(\theta)
\]

for the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood. Let the per-observation Fisher information be

\[
I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\big[S_1(\theta)S_1(\theta)^\top\big],
\]

so the Fisher information in the full sample is

\[
I_n(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\big[S_n(\theta)S_n(\theta)^\top\big]
= n I(\theta).
\]

Assume \(I(\theta)\) is nonsingular.

---

## (i) Cramér–Rao lower bound

Let \(\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R^k\) be differentiable, and let \(T=T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\in\mathbb R^k\) be unbiased for \(\psi(\theta)\), i.e.

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta).
\]

Let \(D\psi(\theta)\) denote the \(k\times d\) Jacobian matrix of \(\psi\). Then the Cramér–Rao lower bound is

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)
\succeq
D\psi(\theta)\, I_n(\theta)^{-1}\, D\psi(\theta)^\top
=
\frac1n D\psi(\theta)\, I(\theta)^{-1}\, D\psi(\theta)^\top .
}
\]

In particular, if \(k=1\), so that \(\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R\), then

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)
\ge
\frac1n \nabla \psi(\theta)^\top I(\theta)^{-1}\nabla \psi(\theta).
}
\]

### Proof

Let \(f_\theta(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i)\) be the joint density. Under the usual regularity conditions, differentiation under the integral sign is allowed.

First,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[S_n(\theta)]
=
\int \nabla_\theta \log f_\theta(x) f_\theta(x)\,dx
=
\int \nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)\,dx
=
\nabla_\theta \int f_\theta(x)\,dx
=
0.
\]

Now since \(T\) is unbiased,

\[
\psi(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta[T]
=
\int T(x) f_\theta(x)\,dx.
\]

Differentiating with respect to \(\theta\),

\[
D\psi(\theta)
=
\int T(x) \nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)^\top\,dx
=
\int T(x) S_n(\theta)^\top f_\theta(x)\,dx.
\]

Since \(\mathbb E_\theta[S_n(\theta)]=0\), this gives

\[
D\psi(\theta)
=
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T,S_n(\theta)).
\]

Also,

\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(S_n(\theta))=I_n(\theta).
\]

Consider the joint covariance matrix of \((T,S_n(\theta))\):

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T) & D\psi(\theta)\\
D\psi(\theta)^\top & I_n(\theta)
\end{pmatrix}
\succeq 0.
\]

Because \(I_n(\theta)\) is nonsingular, the Schur complement is positive semidefinite:

\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)
-
D\psi(\theta) I_n(\theta)^{-1} D\psi(\theta)^\top
\succeq 0.
\]

Thus

\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)
\succeq
D\psi(\theta) I_n(\theta)^{-1}D\psi(\theta)^\top,
\]

which proves the Cramér–Rao lower bound.

---

## (ii) One-step Newton–Raphson estimator and efficiency

Let \(\tilde\theta\) be an initial estimator satisfying

\[
\|\tilde\theta-\theta_0\|_2=o_p(n^{-1/4}).
\]

The Newton–Raphson one-step estimator based on the negative log-likelihood is

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta
=
\tilde\theta
-
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta).
}
\]

Equivalently, since \(S_n(\theta)=-\nabla l_n(\theta)\),

\[
\hat\theta
=
\tilde\theta
+
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}S_n(\tilde\theta).
\]

We show that \(\hat\theta\) is asymptotically normal and efficient.

Assume the usual likelihood regularity conditions:

\[
\frac1n H_n(\theta_0)\xrightarrow{p} I(\theta_0),
\]

with \(I(\theta_0)\) positive definite, and assume that in a neighborhood of \(\theta_0\),

\[
\|H_n(u)-H_n(v)\|_{\text{op}}
\le L_n\|u-v\|_2,
\]

with \(L_n/n=O_p(1)\). This is the natural scaling for a Hessian of a sum of \(n\) log-likelihood contributions.

Let \(\bar\theta_n\) denote the MLE. By the hint, we may assume the MLE is asymptotically efficient:

\[
\sqrt n(\bar\theta_n-\theta_0)
\rightsquigarrow
N_d(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}).
\]

In particular,

\[
\bar\theta_n-\theta_0=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Therefore

\[
\tilde\theta-\bar\theta_n
=
(\tilde\theta-\theta_0)-(\bar\theta_n-\theta_0)
=
o_p(n^{-1/4}).
\]

Set

\[
\delta_n=\tilde\theta-\bar\theta_n.
\]

Because \(\bar\theta_n\) is the MLE, assuming it lies in the interior of the parameter space,

\[
\nabla l_n(\bar\theta_n)=0.
\]

Using Taylor’s theorem with integral remainder,

\[
\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta)
=
\nabla l_n(\bar\theta_n)
+
\left\{
\int_0^1 H_n(\bar\theta_n+t\delta_n)\,dt
\right\}\delta_n.
\]

Since \(\nabla l_n(\bar\theta_n)=0\), define

\[
A_n
=
\int_0^1 H_n(\bar\theta_n+t\delta_n)\,dt,
\]

so that

\[
\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta)=A_n\delta_n.
\]

Then

\[
\hat\theta-\bar\theta_n
=
\tilde\theta-\bar\theta_n
-
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta)
=
\delta_n-H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}A_n\delta_n.
\]

Hence

\[
\hat\theta-\bar\theta_n
=
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}
\{H_n(\tilde\theta)-A_n\}\delta_n.
\]

Now, by the Lipschitz condition,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|H_n(\tilde\theta)-A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
&=
\left\|
\int_0^1
\{H_n(\tilde\theta)-H_n(\bar\theta_n+t\delta_n)\}\,dt
\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\\
&\le
\int_0^1
L_n \|\tilde\theta-(\bar\theta_n+t\delta_n)\|_2\,dt\\
&=
\int_0^1
L_n(1-t)\|\delta_n\|_2\,dt\\
&=
\frac{L_n}{2}\|\delta_n\|_2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Also,

\[
\frac1n H_n(\tilde\theta)
=
\frac1n H_n(\theta_0)
+
\frac1n\{H_n(\tilde\theta)-H_n(\theta_0)\}.
\]

The first term converges in probability to \(I(\theta_0)\), and the second satisfies

\[
\left\|
\frac1n\{H_n(\tilde\theta)-H_n(\theta_0)\}
\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\le
\frac{L_n}{n}\|\tilde\theta-\theta_0\|_2
=
O_p(1)o_p(1)
=
o_p(1).
\]

Thus

\[
\frac1n H_n(\tilde\theta)\xrightarrow{p} I(\theta_0).
\]

Since \(I(\theta_0)\) is positive definite, \(H_n(\tilde\theta)\) is invertible with probability tending to one, and

\[
\|H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_p(n^{-1}).
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\hat\theta-\bar\theta_n\|_2
&\le
\|H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\|H_n(\tilde\theta)-A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\|\delta_n\|_2\\
&\le
O_p(n^{-1})\cdot \frac{L_n}{2}\|\delta_n\|_2^2\\
&=
O_p(L_n/n)\|\delta_n\|_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(L_n/n=O_p(1)\) and \(\|\delta_n\|_2=o_p(n^{-1/4})\),

\[
\|\delta_n\|_2^2=o_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta-\bar\theta_n=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
}
\]

Thus \(\hat\theta\) is first-order asymptotically equivalent to the MLE. Hence

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
=
\sqrt n(\bar\theta_n-\theta_0)
+
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\bar\theta_n)
=
\sqrt n(\bar\theta_n-\theta_0)+o_p(1).
\]

Using the assumed asymptotic efficiency of the MLE,

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
\rightsquigarrow
N_d(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}).
}
\]

Therefore \(\hat\theta\) is asymptotically normal with asymptotic covariance

\[
\frac1n I(\theta_0)^{-1}.
\]

For estimating \(\theta\) itself, the Cramér–Rao lower bound from part (i) is

\[
I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}
=
\frac1n I(\theta_0)^{-1}.
\]

Thus the one-step estimator achieves the Cramér–Rao lower bound asymptotically.

More generally, for estimating \(\psi(\theta)\), define the plug-in estimator

\[
\hat\psi=\psi(\hat\theta).
\]

By the multivariate delta method,

\[
\sqrt n\{\psi(\hat\theta)-\psi(\theta_0)\}
\rightsquigarrow
N_k\left(
0,\,
D\psi(\theta_0)I(\theta_0)^{-1}D\psi(\theta_0)^\top
\right).
\]

Hence

\[
\operatorname{Avar}(\hat\psi)
=
\frac1n
D\psi(\theta_0)I(\theta_0)^{-1}D\psi(\theta_0)^\top,
\]

which equals the Cramér–Rao lower bound from part (i). Therefore the one-step estimator is asymptotically efficient.
